title: Oat flour for all the flour in an egg batter baked to rise by steam

exceptions.reason: A chemically leavened recipe is covered by oat_flour_for_all_flour_not_offered.

evidence.basis: Knowledge packet 2026-10-13b item F, PROPOSED (not approved). Closes the scope gap in R1's oat_flour_for_all_flour_not_offered@1, whose "dough that rises" is encoded as "has a leavener": popovers and Yorkshire pudding rise with none. Sources: America's Test Kitchen, Muffin Tin Popovers (recipe 15310, fetched 2026-10-13): "there's no yeast or chemical leaveners (baking powder or baking soda) in this batter", "these popovers rely on the power of steam to give them a lift", "Using higher-protein bread flour instead of all-purpose means there's enough structure in the popovers"; King Arthur Baking blog, "Never-fail popovers: fact or fiction?" (2010-04-15): "a steam-filled wonder that magically bakes up to nearly triple its original size". The disagreement it carries is R1's (D-5: KA up to half, Bob's Red Mill up to a fifth, Quaker all of it only when the bake doesn't need to rise). ENGINEERING INFERENCE: "an egg batter that is baked" as the detectable sign of a steam-raised bake (eggs are in every steam-raised batter in the sources; a baked recipe with no egg and no leavener, e.g. shortbread, is left to Quaker's "doesn't need to rise"). Not kitchen-tested.

text: CourseCorrect doesn't offer oat flour in place of all the flour in this batter: it rises by steam in the oven, and the flour is its structure. For a bake that has to rise, the sources disagree (King Arthur Baking says up to half, Bob's Red Mill up to a fifth; Quaker allows all of it only when the bake doesn't need to rise).
scopeNote: This is about replacing all of the flour here. It isn't a verdict on oat-flour recipes or on using some oat flour.
answer: isn't offered here, because the sources disagree
